evidence.claim: Its profile emphasizes the historic district’s record of European and African settlement, commerce and industry.

evidence.claim: A 1998 state act designated a ten-mile section north of Church Creek Bridge as a scenic byway and prohibited off-premises outdoor advertising there.
evidence.quote: That portion of South Carolina Highway 61, beginning at Church Creek Bridge and extending for a distance of ten miles north of the bridge, is hereby designated a South Carolina Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: prohibited off-premises outdoor advertising there

evidence.claim: The landscape includes engineered rice fields: at Magnolia, enslaved Africans from rice-growing regions built the dams and dikes used to irrigate the crop.
evidence.quote: Magnolia was originally a rice plantation, with extensive earthworks of dams and dikes built in fields along the river for irrigating land for rice cultivation. African enslaved people from rice-growing regions created the works.

evidence.claim: The river had served as a primary transportation route, carrying goods as well as people through the Lowcountry.
evidence.quote: Historically, the Wando, Cooper, Ashley, Stono, and Edisto rivers served as the primary transportation routes in the Lowcountry. These waterways were used for exploration and settlement, the movement of goods, and the cultivation of staple crops.

evidence.claim: Traveling toward Charleston, begin with Middleton Place’s riverbank gardens.
evidence.quote: Ashley River Road (part of South Carolina Highway 61), which connects Middleton Place to Charleston to the southeast and the Legend Oaks area to the northwest

evidence.claim: Middleton Place’s riverbank gardens
evidence.quote: The east gardens stretch eastward from the main residence for approximately 200 feet (61 m) before descending in a series of terraces to the floodplain of the Ashley River.

evidence.claim: Middleton Place’s Butterfly Lakes lie beneath terraces descending toward the Ashley River.
evidence.quote: Two congruent ponds at the eastern base of the terraces resemble butterfly wings, and are thus known as the "Butterfly Lakes".

evidence.claim: The gardens were rebuilt over decades after John Julius Pringle Smith and his wife Heningham began restoring them in 1916.
evidence.quote: The restoration of Middleton Place began in 1916 when Middleton descendant John Julius Pringle Smith (1887–1969) and his wife Heningham began several decades' work of meticulously rebuilding the plantation's gardens.

evidence.claim: The main house did not survive: Union soldiers burned it in 1865, and the 1886 earthquake brought down its remaining walls.
evidence.quote: In 1865, toward the end of the American Civil War, Union soldiers burned most of the house

evidence.claim: the 1886 earthquake brought down its remaining walls
evidence.quote: The 1886 Charleston earthquake toppled the walls of the main house and north wing.

evidence.claim: The present house was the south wing, repaired and converted into a residence after the war.
evidence.quote: In 1868, Williams Middleton restored the roof to the south flanker at Middleton Place, and converted it to the main residence.

evidence.claim: The Middleton Place Foundation has researched the thousands of African Americans enslaved by the Middleton family.
evidence.quote: the Middleton Place Foundation has carried out extensive research to document the thousands of African-American slaves once owned by the Middleton family.

evidence.claim: Bricks salvaged from the ruined main house were reused in the later stableyard complex.
evidence.quote: the buildings were constructed of brick salvaged from the ruined main house.

evidence.claim: The paired Butterfly Lakes resemble wings at the base of the garden terraces.
evidence.quote: Two congruent ponds at the eastern base of the terraces resemble butterfly wings

evidence.claim: Drayton Hall’s double projecting portico faces the land approach from Ashley River Road, away from the river.
evidence.quote: The house has a double projecting portico on the west facade, which faces away from the river and toward the land side approach from Ashley River Road.

evidence.claim: Inside, a central entrance hall and divided staircase lead to a large salon, with chambers to either side.
evidence.quote: A large central entrance stair hall with a symmetrical divided staircase is backed by a large salon, flanked by square and rectangular chambers.

evidence.claim: Its architecture follows Palladian models, including the symmetrical arrangement of the entrance hall, salon and surrounding rooms.
evidence.quote: The floor plan is Palladian-inspired as well

evidence.claim: The house belonged to an indigo and rice plantation whose grounds included thirteen cabins for enslaved people.
evidence.quote: part of the plantation based on indigo and rice and the former site of 13 slave cabins

evidence.claim: Seven generations of Drayton heirs preserved the house, but its flanking service buildings were lost.
evidence.quote: Seven generations of Drayton heirs preserved the house, though the flanking outbuildings have not survived

evidence.claim: An earthquake destroyed the laundry in 1886; a hurricane destroyed the kitchen in 1893.
evidence.quote: an earthquake destroyed the laundry house in 1886, and a hurricane destroyed the kitchen in 1893.

evidence.claim: The double portico faces the road approach, away from the Ashley River.
evidence.quote: The house has a double projecting portico on the west facade, which faces away from the river and toward the land side approach from Ashley River Road.

evidence.claim: Old St. Andrew’s began as a rectangular brick church in 1706; an expansion starting in 1723 turned it into a cross.
evidence.quote: Beginning in 1723 and continuing for more than a decade, the small, rectangular church was expanded into the shape of a cross.

evidence.claim: rectangular brick church in 1706
evidence.quote: St. Andrew's Parish Church was built in 1706. It was forty feet long and twenty-five feet wide, built of brick

evidence.claim: The enlarged building tripled the floor space.
evidence.quote: The expansion tripled the floor space of the existing church.

evidence.claim: Stucco concealed differences between the old and new brickwork and imitated a stone facade.
evidence.quote: The exterior brick was roughcast or stuccoed to mask the differences between the old and new brick and emulate a grander stone facade.

evidence.claim: A fire in the early 1760s left the walls standing, and the restored church reopened in 1764.
evidence.quote: It was severe enough that anything made of wood would have burned, leaving the 1706 and 1723 walls standing. The church was thoroughly restored and reopened in 1764.

evidence.claim: A fire in the early 1760s
evidence.quote: a devastating fire struck the church in the early 1760s.

evidence.claim: Its altarpiece dates from that rebuilding.
evidence.quote: Features of the 1764 rebuilding include the magnificent reredos or altarpiece at the east end

evidence.claim: The fire restoration also gave the church its west-end balcony and stone-and-tile floor.
evidence.quote: Features of the 1764 rebuilding include the magnificent reredos or altarpiece at the east end, the balcony at the west end, the stone and tile paver floor throughout the church

evidence.claim: The building remains in use for worship, retaining features of several periods of enlargement and repair.
evidence.quote: Old St. Andrew's, as it is commonly called, remains an active place of worship
